newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: El Nino could be costly, warn scientists.
newsitem.headline: El Nino could be costly, warn scientists.

text.p: International scientists warned on Wednesday that a major El Nino weather pattern was occurring with the potential to cause billions of dollars of damage in key agricultural regions worldwide.

Meteorogical and oceanographic readings from the tropical Pacific ocean point to formation of an El Nino possibly rivalling the one in 1982 and 1983, the largest this century, which was responsible for hurricanes, droughts, fires and flooding in over 15 countries.

"In places like Australia and South America, the effects could be devastating," Keven Trenberth head of the climate analysis arm of the U.S. Weather Service's National Center for Atmospheric Research told Reuters.

Meteorologists meeting in Melbourne this week to discuss the climate said producers of agricultural commodities such as coffee, wheat, sugar and other staples were at greatest risk from an El Nino, which typically causes droughts in some parts of the world and floods in others.
Industries that depend on hydro-power to operate are also at risk, as are inland shipping lanes that require navigable water levels to ferry supplies to remote mine sites.
In places such as Papua New Guinea and in East Kalimantan, Indonesia, such vessels have been marooned for weeks at a time on dry river beds.

An El Nino, which is Spanish for Christ Child because it normally occurs around Christmas, forms when waters in the tropical Pacific ocean turn warmer, changing wind and other global patterns -- which in turn wreaks havoc on weather sensitive regions.
But there is strong evidence that the next El Nino has arrived early, which means it could last longer than previous ones.

"The central and Eastern Pacific equatorial Pacific Ocean became warmer and the trade winds across most of the tropical Pacific are much weaker than normal," said Bill Kininmonth, head of the climate centre of the Australian Bureau of Meteorology.
This and other data indicate the latest El Nino is the strongest since 1983, he said.
Australian farmers and ranchers are being warned to brace for drought conditions, which threaten everything from wheat and canola to raising of livestock.
In 1983, thousands of head of livstock in Australia were destroyed because there was no grain feed for them to eat.
"It was a terrible time of severe drought and economic impact," said John Kermond of the Washington-based National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAC).
According to NOAC, the 1982-83 El Nino wreaked economic damage costing at least US$8 billion.

At the Coffee Sugar and Cocoa Exchange in New York, cocoa prices rose recently on worries about possible crop damage in Indonesia and elsewhere due to the El Nino as temperatures rise in the southern hemisphere.

Oil World, an independent agricutural newsletter has said there is a 50 percent chance the U.S., Europe, and Africa would be negatively affected by El Nino, while there is a 60 to 80 percent chance of droughts in Oceania and Asia.
There is little to suggest that an El Nino is anthing more than a naturally recurring phenomenum, although some scientits have suggested a link with global warming.
They noted what seems to be increasing frequency in which they occur.
"El Ninos have been going on for thousands of years, but now there seems to be more than ever," said Trenbeth of the National Center for Atmospheric Research.
